intro: A spoon of sugar vanishes into tea. A puddle dries up and leaves nothing behind. A balloon that looks empty pushes back when you squeeze it. A friend across a noisy gym reads a message you sent with nothing but a blinking flashlight. Each of these is a puzzle about things you cannot see.

This unit gives you tools to solve those puzzles. The first tool is a balance. With it you will prove that sugar, air and melted ice are still there, even when your eyes say otherwise. The second tool is a picture in your mind: matter as tiny particles, always moving, never lost.

Then you will follow the patterns that move through matter: waves in a rope, sound in the air, light bouncing off a mirror or bending in water. By the end, you will be able to explain why a straw looks broken in a glass, how a code turns blinks into words, and why a text message crosses the world without a single wrong letter.
bigQuestion: How can we know what matter is made of and what waves carry, when both are too small or too fast to see?

timeline.t: Democritus argues that everything is made of tiny pieces moving in empty space
Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics: we see because light enters the eye
Isaac Newton reports that a prism splits white sunlight into colors
Antoine Lavoisier shows with careful weighing that mass is conserved in every change
John Dalton explains chemical changes as rearrangements of atoms
Robert Brown sees pollen grains jiggle in water, a clue to unseen moving particles
Samuel Morse sends the first public telegraph message in dots and dashes
Alexander Graham Bell's telephone turns a voice into an electric signal
Albert Einstein explains the jiggling pollen as kicks from invisible water particles
The scanning tunneling microscope lets scientists make pictures of single atoms

words.d: anything that has mass and takes up space
the amount of stuff in an object, measured with a balance
one of the tiny pieces that all matter is made of
the rule that the total amount of matter stays the same through a change
to break into particles so small they spread through a liquid and cannot be seen
a feature of a material that you can observe or measure
a change that makes new substances with new properties
a repeating pattern of motion that carries energy through a material
the height of a wave; a measure of its energy
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the bending of light when it passes from one material into another
a code that uses only two signals, on and off, written as 1 and 0

test.why: Air has mass and takes up space. Light, shadows and songs do not have mass.

test.q: Why do scientists use a particle model?
choices: Models are easier to draw than real things
Particles are real but far too small to see
Models replace the need for experiments
test.why: A model stands in for something real we cannot see directly. Particles are real but tiny.

test.q: A sealed bag of ice is weighed, melts, and is weighed again. The mass:
test.why: Melting changes solid to liquid but no particles leave the sealed bag.

test.q: A student stirs salt into water until it vanishes. The salt:
choices: Is still there, spread out as tiny particles
test.why: The salt dissolved. Its particles are too small to see, but the mass and the taste prove they are there.

test.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz in an open cup and the mass drops. The best explanation is:
choices: A gas escaped into the air
test.why: The bubbles are a gas. When they pop and float away, they take their mass with them.

test.q: Which is a property you could use to identify a material?
test.why: Magnetism is a feature of the material itself that you can test. Price and age are not properties of the material.

test.q: Which change makes a new substance?
test.why: The fizz is carbon dioxide, a new substance with new properties. The other changes can be undone.

test.q: A wave passes a floating leaf. The leaf:
choices: Bobs up and down and stays near its spot
test.why: Waves move the water up and down. The energy travels on, but the water and the leaf stay close.

test.q: A wave with a bigger amplitude:
test.why: Amplitude is the height of a wave, and a taller wave carries more energy.

test.q: You hold a paper near a loud speaker and it flutters. This shows that:
choices: Sound waves carry energy that can move objects
Light from the speaker pushes the paper
test.why: Sound is a wave of pushes in the air. Its energy reached the paper and moved it.

test.q: In a completely dark room you cannot see a chair because:
choices: No light reflects off the chair into your eyes
test.why: Seeing needs light bouncing off an object into your eyes. With no light, nothing reaches them.

test.q: A straw in a glass of water looks broken because:
choices: Light bends as it passes from water into air
The water pushes the straw sideways
test.why: Refraction bends the light from the underwater part, so your eye sees it in the wrong place.

test.q: In Morse code, the letter O is:
test.why: O is three long signals, or dashes. S is three dots.

test.q: With 4 bits, how many different patterns can you make?
test.why: Each added bit doubles the count: 2, 4, 8, 16.

test.q: Why can a digital message cross an ocean without errors?
choices: Bits are sent as light only
Receivers only decide on or off and send fresh copies
test.why: Even a weak flash is clearly on, not off. A receiver copies the bits cleanly and sends them on.

write.prompt: Make a claim: when sugar disappears into water, is the sugar still there? Support it with evidence from the balance test and from what happens when the water dries. Then explain how the particle model makes sense of that evidence.
tips: Claim: say clearly whether the sugar is still there and in what form.
Evidence: use the mass before and after stirring, and the crystals left after drying.
Reasoning: explain how particles too small to see can still have mass and be tasted.
The other side: what would someone who thinks the sugar is gone expect the balance to show?
Compare: how is this different from baking soda fizzing in vinegar?

title: Matter and Waves

chapters.title: Particles Too Small to See
chapters.bigQuestion: If matter is made of pieces too small to see, how can we prove those pieces are still there?

story.title: The Sugar That Disappeared
story.kicker: A spoon of sugar vanishes into a cup of tea. Did it stop existing, or just hide?
paragraphs: Maya's grandmother made tea every afternoon in her apartment in Chicago. One day Maya watched her stir a spoonful of sugar into the cup. The white crystals swirled, got smaller, and then were gone. The tea looked exactly like plain tea. "Where did the sugar go?" Maya asked. Her grandmother smiled and handed her the cup. "Taste it."

The tea was sweet. The sugar was gone from sight, but it was not gone from the cup. Maya could taste it in every sip. That bothered her. How can something be in a cup and still be invisible? She decided to run a test the next day at school.

Her class had a balance, the kind with two pans. Maya put a cup of water on one pan and a small pile of sugar next to it. She added weights to the other pan until the pans hung level. Then she stirred the sugar into the water until it vanished. She set the cup back on the pan. The pans stayed level. Nothing had been lost.

Her teacher explained the idea. Sugar is made of particles far too small to see. Stirring breaks the crystals apart and spreads those particles between the water particles. They are still there, every one of them. That is why the balance did not change, and why the tea was sweet.

Maya poured a little of the sweet water onto a plate and left it by a sunny window. Two days later the water was gone. A crust of tiny white crystals sat on the plate. She touched one to her tongue. Sugar. It had never left.
story.think: Maya's test used a balance. What could she have concluded if the pans had NOT stayed level after she stirred?

lessons.title: What Counts as Matter
lessons.mainIdea: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, and that includes things you cannot see, like air.
reading: Pick up a rock. It feels heavy, and it fills your hand. Now think about the air in the room. You cannot see it, and it does not feel heavy. Yet the rock and the air have something in common. Both are *matter*. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.

*Mass* is the amount of stuff in an object. A balance measures mass by comparing an object to known weights. A bowling ball has more mass than a tennis ball. A cup of water has more mass than an empty cup. Mass does not change when you carry an object to a new place.

Air is the tricky one. Push an empty cup upside down into a sink full of water. The water does not fill the cup. Something is already inside, pushing back. That something is air. Air takes up space. Later in this chapter you will see that air has mass too.

words.d: anything that has mass and takes up space
the amount of stuff in an object, measured with a balance

look.title: The Upside-Down Cup
look.text: A student pushes an empty glass straight down into a bucket of water, open end first. The inside of the glass stays dry. Then she tilts the glass a little. A big bubble wobbles out and rises to the surface. Now water fills more of the glass.
look.prompt: What was the bubble made of, and where was it before the glass tipped? What does this show about air?

check.q: Which of these is matter?
check.why: Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. A shadow, a color and an idea have no mass.

check.q: A student carries a rock from Chicago to Springfield. What happens to its mass?
check.why: Mass is the amount of stuff in an object. Moving the rock does not add or remove any stuff.

check.q: Why does water not rush into a cup pushed upside down into a sink?
choices: Air inside the cup takes up the space
check.why: The cup is not empty. It is full of air, and the air takes up space, so the water cannot get in.

lessons.title: Pieces Too Small to See
lessons.mainIdea: All matter is made of particles far too small to see, and a model helps us picture how they are arranged.
reading: Tear a piece of paper in half. Tear it again, and again. Soon the pieces are too small to tear. Now imagine a tool a million times sharper. You could keep going until you reached the smallest pieces of the paper. Scientists call these tiny pieces *particles*. Every kind of matter is made of them.

Particles are so small that no eye can see one. No classroom microscope can either. A single drop of water holds more particles than there are people on Earth. Many times more. Because we cannot see them, scientists use a *model*. A model is a picture or idea that stands in for something real.

Here is a simple particle model. In a solid, the particles are packed tight and only jiggle in place. In a liquid, they stay close but slide past each other. In a gas, they fly apart and zoom around. Try this model on ice, water and steam. It is the same water, with the particles moving in three different ways.

words.d: one of the tiny pieces that all matter is made of
a picture or idea that stands in for something real that is hard to see

look.title: An Old Idea About Tiny Pieces
look.text: More than 2,000 years ago, the Greek thinker Democritus argued that everything is built from tiny pieces that cannot be split, moving through empty space. He said that sweetness, bitterness and color are only how these pieces seem to us. In truth, he claimed, there are only the pieces and the empty space between them.
look.cite: Democritus of Abdera, as reported by later Greek writers, about 400 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Democritus had no microscope. What everyday observations might have made him think matter comes in tiny pieces?

check.q: Why do scientists use a model to explain particles?
choices: Models are more fun than experiments
Particles are far too small to see
check.why: A model stands in for something real that we cannot see directly. Particles are real but much too small to see.

check.q: In the particle model, how do particles move in a solid?
choices: They fly apart and zoom around
They do not exist in solids
check.why: In a solid the particles are packed tight and can only jiggle where they are.

check.q: Ice melts into water and then boils into steam. What happens to the particles?
choices: They are the same particles, moving differently
check.why: Ice, water and steam are the same water. Only the way the particles move and space out changes.

lessons.title: A Balloon on the Balance
lessons.mainIdea: A gas is matter: it has mass and takes up space, and a careful balance can prove it.
reading: A *gas* is matter whose particles spread out to fill any space they are given. Air is a mix of gases. Because you cannot see air, it is easy to believe it weighs nothing. A *balance* says otherwise. Here is a test you can do with a stick, some string and two balloons.

Blow up one balloon as big as you can and tie it. Hang it from one end of the stick, and hang a matching empty balloon from the other end. Slide the string until the stick hangs level. Now pop the full balloon with a pin. The end with the empty balloon drops, and the popped side rises. The air that escaped had mass.

The difference is small, because a balloon holds only a little air. A whole room is another story. The air in a classroom can have a mass of more than 100 kilograms, more than the mass of an adult. You walk through it every day without noticing.

words.d: matter whose particles spread out to fill any space they are given
a tool that compares the mass of two things

look.title: Mass of One Liter of Different Materials
look.prompt: Air has mass, but very little per liter. How does this table help explain why people once believed air weighed nothing?

check.q: A stick balances two balloons. One is popped. What happens?
check.why: The air that escaped had mass. With less mass on that side, the popped side rises.

check.q: Which statement about a gas is true?
choices: A gas keeps a fixed shape
A gas fills any space it is given
check.why: Gas particles spread out to fill whatever container they are in. A gas is matter and does have mass.

check.q: Why is the mass of the air in a balloon hard to notice?
choices: A balloon holds only a little air
Air loses its mass inside rubber
check.why: One liter of air has a mass of only about 1 gram. A balloon holds just a few liters, so the mass is small.

lessons.title: Ice Melts, Mass Stays
lessons.mainIdea: When a solid melts or a liquid freezes, its shape and look change, but the amount of matter does not.
reading: Put some ice cubes in a sealed plastic bag and set it on a balance. Write down the mass. Leave the bag in a warm spot. An hour later the ice is a puddle inside the bag. Put it back on the balance. The reading is the same. Melting changed the ice from solid to liquid, but no particles left the bag.

This is what the particle model predicts. When ice *melts*, warmth makes its particles jiggle faster. They break out of their tight pattern and begin to slide past each other. The same particles are still there. They are just moving more freely. None are made and none are lost.

The rule works the other way too. Freeze the bag and the mass stays the same. Scientists call this idea *conservation* of mass. Conservation means the total stays the same. It is one of the most tested ideas in all of science, and it has passed every fair test.

words.d: to change from a solid to a liquid when warmed
when a total amount stays the same through a change

look.title: The Frozen Water Bottle
look.text: A student fills a plastic bottle with water, caps it tightly and weighs it. She puts it in the freezer overnight. In the morning the water is solid ice and the bottle has bulged out on the sides. She weighs it again before it can thaw.
look.prompt: The bottle looks different and takes up more space. Predict what the balance shows. What would change your mind?

check.q: A sealed bag of ice has a mass of 50 grams. After the ice melts, what is the mass?
check.why: Melting does not add or remove particles. The same water is in the bag, so the mass stays 50 grams.

check.q: What happens to the particles in ice when it melts?
choices: They jiggle faster and slide past each other
check.why: Warmth makes the particles move faster until they can slide past one another, which is a liquid.

check.q: Why do scientists trust the idea of conservation of mass so much?
choices: It has passed every fair test
check.why: Science trusts ideas that keep passing tests. Conservation of mass has been tested many times.

lessons.title: Where the Sugar Went
lessons.mainIdea: When a solid dissolves, its particles spread out between the liquid's particles; the solid is still there, and the mass proves it.
reading: Drop a sugar cube into warm water and stir. The cube shrinks and then vanishes. The water stays clear. Has the sugar stopped existing? Taste the water and you have your answer. It is sweet. The sugar *dissolved*. To dissolve means to break into particles so small they spread all through a liquid and cannot be seen.

The balance agrees with your tongue. Weigh a cup of water and a spoon of sugar together before you mix them. Weigh them again after the sugar dissolves. The mass is the same. Every particle of sugar is still in the cup, just spread out. Salt does the same thing. So does drink powder.

You can even get the sugar back. Pour a little of the sweet water onto a dark plate. Leave it in a warm, dry place for a few days. The water slowly changes into a gas and drifts away. The sugar cannot do that. It stays behind and builds up into tiny *crystals*. Dissolving hides the sugar, but it does not destroy it.

words.d: to break into particles so small they spread through a liquid and cannot be seen
a solid piece with a regular shape, like a grain of sugar or salt

look.title: Salt on a Winter Street
look.text: In January, trucks spread salt on Chicago streets. By afternoon the snow has turned to slush and the salt crystals are gone. A week later, after the slush has dried up, white streaks appear on the black pavement and on people's boots.
look.prompt: Where was the salt during the week when nobody could see it? What are the white streaks made of?

check.q: Sugar dissolves in water. What happened to the sugar?
choices: It floated away as a gas
Its particles spread through the water
check.why: Dissolving breaks the sugar into particles too small to see, but they are all still in the water.

check.q: A cup of water and a spoon of salt have a total mass of 210 grams. After the salt dissolves, the cup has a mass of:
check.why: No salt left the cup, so the mass of water plus salt is unchanged.

check.q: How can you get dissolved sugar out of water?
check.why: Water can leave as a gas, but sugar cannot. Let the water dry away and sugar crystals are left behind.

lessons.title: Mixing Adds Up
lessons.mainIdea: When you mix two materials, the mass of the mixture equals the mass of the parts you put in.
reading: A *mixture* is two or more materials stirred together while each keeps its own particles. Sand and gravel make a mixture. So do salt and pepper, or trail mix. The pieces might be big or too small to see, but nothing new is made. With patience, you could sort them out again.

Weigh a cup of sand. Weigh a cup of pebbles. Add the two numbers to get a *total*. Now pour them together and weigh the mixture. The balance matches your total. It works with water and food coloring too. The color spreads everywhere, but the balance reads exactly the water plus the drops.

This is conservation of mass again. Mixing moves particles around, but it does not make particles appear or disappear. When a measurement seems to break this rule, scientists get curious. Almost always, some matter slipped away where nobody was looking. The next lesson shows how.

words.d: two or more materials together, with each keeping its own particles
the amount you get when you add everything together

look.title: The Trail Mix Bag
look.text: A student weighs 40 grams of raisins, 60 grams of peanuts and 30 grams of pretzels. She pours all three into one bag and shakes it hard. Before she weighs the bag, her friend says the mix will be lighter now because the pretzels got crushed into crumbs.
look.prompt: What will the balance show for the full bag? Explain why the friend's idea is wrong.

check.q: You mix 100 grams of sand with 50 grams of pebbles. What is the mass of the mixture?
choices: It depends on how well you stir
check.why: Mixing only moves particles around. The total is 100 plus 50, or 150 grams.

check.q: Which of these is a mixture?
check.why: In salt and pepper, each material keeps its own particles. The others are single materials.

check.q: A measurement seems to show mass disappearing during mixing. What do scientists usually find?
choices: The rule of conservation has failed
check.why: Conservation of mass has passed every fair test. Usually a gas or a spill got away unseen.

lessons.title: When the Balance Seems Wrong
lessons.mainIdea: If mass seems to vanish during a change, matter has usually escaped as a gas; a closed container catches it.
reading: Pour vinegar into a cup of baking soda. It fizzes and foams. Weigh the cup before and after. This time the balance reading drops! Was matter destroyed? Look at the fizz. Bubbles rose and popped. A gas formed and floated out of the cup into the room. The missing mass left with that gas.

Try it again in a bottle with a balloon stretched over the top. Put the baking soda in the balloon and the vinegar in the bottle. Weigh it all. Then lift the balloon so the powder falls in. The balloon puffs up with the new gas. Weigh it again. Now the mass is the same. Nothing got out, so nothing was lost.

A container that lets nothing in or out is called a *closed system*. In a closed system, mass never changes, no matter what happens inside. When a puddle *evaporates* and disappears, the water became a gas and joined the air. The world's water has not shrunk. It has only moved.

words.d: a container that lets no matter in or out
to change from a liquid into a gas and drift away

look.title: Lavoisier Weighs Everything
look.text: In 1789, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier wrote that in every change, whether made by nature or by people, nothing is created and nothing is destroyed. The same amount of matter exists before and after the change. He weighed the ingredients and the results of his experiments in sealed vessels to show it.
look.cite: Antoine Lavoisier, Elementary Treatise on Chemistry, 1789 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Lavoisier used careful weighing in sealed containers. Why did sealed containers matter so much for his rule?

check.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz in an open cup, and the mass drops. Why?
choices: A gas escaped into the air
check.why: The bubbles are a gas. When they pop, the gas leaves the cup and takes its mass with it.

check.q: The same fizz happens inside a bottle sealed with a balloon. What does the balance show?
check.why: The balloon traps the gas. Nothing leaves, so the mass stays the same. This is a closed system.

check.q: A puddle on the sidewalk is gone by afternoon. Where did the water go?
choices: It soaked into the air as nothing
It became a gas and joined the air
check.why: The puddle evaporated. The water particles are now spread out in the air as water vapor.

lessons.title: Properties You Can Test
lessons.mainIdea: A property is something you can observe or measure about a material, and properties let you tell one material from another.
reading: Two white powders sit in cups. One is sugar and one is salt. They look alike. How can you tell them apart without tasting? You test their properties. A *property* is a feature you can observe or measure. Color, shine, hardness and how a material acts near a magnet are all properties.

*Hardness* is how well a material resists being scratched. Try to scratch a penny with your fingernail. You cannot. Try to scratch a piece of chalk. You can. Steel scratches glass, and diamond scratches steel. Scientists rank minerals by hardness on a scale from 1 to 10, with diamond at the top.

*Magnetism* is another quick test. Hold a magnet near a paper clip and the clip jumps. Hold it near an aluminum can and nothing happens. Iron and steel are pulled by magnets; most other metals are not. A magnet is a fast way to sort a pile of mixed metal scraps.

words.d: a feature of a material that you can observe or measure
how well a material resists being scratched
the pull a magnet has on iron, steel and a few other metals

look.title: Mohs Hardness Scale
look.prompt: A mystery mineral scratches calcite but is scratched by fluorite. About where does it sit on the scale? How do you know?

check.q: Which of these is a property of a material?
check.why: A property is a feature you can observe or measure about the material itself, like hardness.

check.q: Material A scratches material B. Which is harder?
check.why: The harder material leaves a scratch on the softer one. A scratched B, so A is harder.

check.q: A magnet picks up one metal scrap but not another. What can you conclude?
choices: The picked-up scrap is likely iron or steel
The other scrap is not a metal
check.why: Magnets pull on iron and steel. Most other metals, like aluminum and copper, are not pulled.

lessons.title: Conduct, Dissolve, Float
lessons.mainIdea: Whether a material carries electricity or heat, dissolves in water, or floats are properties you can test to identify it.
reading: Some materials let electricity flow through them. Copper wire does; a rubber eraser does not. This property is called *conductivity*. Metals are good conductors of electricity. Many are also good conductors of heat. That is why a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot fast, and a wooden spoon does not.

*Solubility* is whether a material dissolves in a liquid. Salt and sugar are soluble in water. Sand and chalk are not. The amount matters too. Water can hold a lot of sugar but much less baking soda. Testing how much dissolves is one safe way to tell white powders apart.

Whether something floats in water is a property as well. Wood floats; a steel nail sinks. This depends on how much mass is packed into a given space. Put several properties together and you have a fingerprint for a material. Detectives, doctors and engineers all identify materials this way.

words.d: how well a material lets electricity or heat pass through it
whether, and how much, a material dissolves in a liquid

look.title: How Much Dissolves in 100 Grams of Room-Temperature Water
look.prompt: You have two unlabeled white powders. Using only water and a spoon, how could this table help you tell sugar from baking soda?

check.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot soup get hot quickly?
check.why: Metals are good conductors. Heat passes through them quickly, unlike wood or plastic.

check.q: Which material is NOT soluble in water?
check.why: Sand does not dissolve. It sinks and stays as grains. The other three spread out and disappear.

check.q: Two clear liquids look the same. Which test would help tell them apart?
check.why: Conductivity is a property of the material. Two different liquids may conduct differently.

lessons.title: Some Mixtures Come Apart
lessons.mainIdea: Salt and water make a mixture, not a new substance; the salt can be taken back out unchanged.
reading: Stir salt into water and it disappears. Yet nothing new has been made. The salt particles and the water particles simply sit side by side. This is a mixture. You can prove it by getting the salt back. Boil the water away, and salt crystals are left in the pan. They taste like salt and look like salt.

A *substance* is one pure kind of matter with its own set of properties. Salt is a substance. Water is a substance. Salt water is a mixture of two substances. Its properties are a blend. It is wet like water and salty like salt. That is a sign that nothing new formed.

Ocean water is a huge natural mixture. People near the sea have collected salt from it for thousands of years by letting the sun dry shallow pools. Closer to home, when winter road salt washes into a river, the salt is still salt. Mixing did not change what it is. You could *separate* it out again.

words.d: one pure kind of matter with its own set of properties
to take a mixture apart into the materials that went into it

look.title: Two Beakers
look.text: Beaker A holds sand stirred into water. In a minute the sand settles on the bottom. Beaker B holds salt stirred into water. It stays clear no matter how long it sits. A student says the salt must have turned into water.
look.prompt: How could you show the student, without tasting, that the salt is still salt and can be separated out?

check.q: Salt water is best described as:
check.why: Salt and water keep their own particles and sit side by side. That makes salt water a mixture.

check.q: How can you separate salt from salt water?
choices: Let the water dry or boil away
check.why: Water leaves as a gas, but salt cannot. When the water is gone, salt crystals remain.

check.q: Which is a sign that mixing did NOT make a new substance?
choices: The parts can be separated again unchanged
check.why: If the original materials can be taken back out unchanged, they only mixed. Bubbles, heat and new colors are clues of something new.

lessons.title: Fizz Means Something New
lessons.mainIdea: Some mixing makes new substances with new properties; bubbles, a color change or a temperature change are clues that this has happened.
reading: Now mix baking soda and vinegar. This time the change is different. The mix fizzes, bubbles pour out, and the cup turns cold. When the fizzing stops, the baking soda is gone, and drying the liquid will not bring it back. Something new was made. The bubbles are *carbon dioxide*, the same gas that makes soda pop fizz.

When mixing makes new substances, we call it a *chemical change*. The particles rearrange into different groups. The new substances have their own properties. Baking soda is a powder that does not fizz by itself. Carbon dioxide is a gas that can put out a candle flame. New properties mean new substances.

Clues of a chemical change are bubbles, a new color, a new smell, or a change in temperature. Rust forming on a bike is a chemical change. So is bread rising in the oven. Not every clue is certain, so scientists test what was made. And in a closed container, the total mass still stays the same, even here.

words.d: a change in which mixing or heating makes new substances with new properties
an invisible gas made when baking soda meets vinegar; it also makes soda fizz

look.title: Cake in the Oven
look.text: A baker mixes flour, sugar, eggs, butter and a spoon of baking soda into a thick batter. In the oven the batter puffs up, turns golden brown and fills the kitchen with a new smell. The baker cannot pull the eggs or the flour back out of the finished cake.
look.prompt: Which clues in this scene point to a chemical change? Which clue is the strongest, and why?

check.q: What are the bubbles when baking soda meets vinegar?
choices: Air that was trapped in the powder
A new gas called carbon dioxide
check.why: The fizz is carbon dioxide, a new substance made by the chemical change. The cup even gets cold, not hot.

check.q: Which is the best sign that a chemical change happened?
choices: The parts can be sorted back out
A new substance with new properties formed
The mass in a closed container changed
check.why: A chemical change makes new substances with new properties. Mass in a closed container never changes.

check.q: Salt dissolving in water and baking soda fizzing in vinegar are different because:
choices: Only the fizz makes a new substance
Only the salt makes a new substance
check.why: Dissolved salt can be taken back out unchanged. Baking soda and vinegar make carbon dioxide and other new substances.

review.why: Air has mass and takes up space. Light, sound and feelings have no mass.

review.q: Why can't you see the particles that water is made of?
review.why: Water particles are real but so small that no classroom microscope can show one.

review.q: A sealed bag of ice cubes is weighed, then left to melt. When weighed again, its mass is:
review.why: Melting changes solid to liquid but adds or removes no particles. The mass stays the same.

review.q: Sugar stirred into tea seems to disappear. What really happened?
choices: Its particles spread through the tea
It floated away as a gas
review.why: The sugar dissolved. Its particles are too small to see, but they are all still there, and the tea is sweet.

review.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz in an open cup and the mass drops. In a sealed bottle, the mass:
review.why: The gas that escaped from the open cup is trapped in the sealed bottle, so nothing is lost.

review.q: Which test would best tell iron nails from aluminum nails?
review.why: Magnets pull on iron but not on aluminum. Magnetism is a fast, safe property test.

review.q: A powder dissolves in water and can be dried back out unchanged. This was:
choices: A mixture, not a new substance
review.why: If the original material comes back unchanged, the particles only mixed. No new substance was made.

review.q: Which clue most strongly suggests a chemical change?
choices: Bubbles of a new gas appear
The mass stays the same in a closed jar
The pieces settle to the bottom
review.why: A new gas is a new substance with new properties. The mass staying the same happens in every change.

chapters.title: Waves, Light and Information
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a wave, a beam of light or a pattern of beats carry something from one place to another?

story.title: A Message Across the Gym
story.kicker: Two friends, one flashlight, and a code that turns blinks into words.
paragraphs: The gym at Jamal's school in Illinois was big and loud. On rainy days the whole class had indoor recess there. Jamal's best friend Rosa was at the far end, and yelling did no good. So Jamal brought a flashlight from home. He had learned something over the weekend, and he wanted to try it.

He pointed the flashlight at the wall near Rosa and clicked it: short, short, short. Then three long flashes. Then three short ones again. Rosa stared. Then she grinned. She had learned the same thing. Short-short-short, long-long-long, short-short-short is the most famous emergency signal in the world: SOS.

Rosa did not have a flashlight, so she used her hands. She thumped the wooden bleacher: three quick taps, three slow taps, three quick taps. Jamal felt it before he heard it, a buzz through the wood. Sound had crossed the gym as a wave, just as the light had. Neither the light nor the sound was a thing you could hold. Each was a pattern, moving.

By the end of recess they had worked out signals for "yes," "no," and "meet me at the door." Nothing traveled across the gym except light and sound. No paper, no phone, no runner. Yet the message got through. That is what waves can do. They carry patterns, and patterns can carry meaning.
story.think: Jamal's flashlight blinks and Rosa's taps carried the same message. What did the two signals have in common, and what was different?

lessons.title: Waves in a Rope and a Pond
lessons.mainIdea: A wave is a repeating pattern of motion that moves energy from place to place while the material itself stays put.
reading: Tie one end of a jump rope to a doorknob. Pull it tight and snap your wrist up and down. A bump races along the rope to the door. The rope did not travel. Each piece of rope moved up and down, then came back. The bump is a *wave*. A wave is a pattern that moves through something.

Drop a pebble in a still pond. Rings spread outward. Now watch a leaf floating nearby. As the rings pass, the leaf bobs up and down. It does not race away with the rings. Water waves move the water up and down, and the pattern rolls on. The water stays close to where it was.

What travels with the wave is *energy*. Energy is the ability to make things move or change. A big wave on Lake Michigan can toss a boat and push sand up the beach. The water in that wave did not come all the way across the lake. The energy in the wave did.

words.d: a repeating pattern of motion that moves through water, air, a rope or another material
the ability to make things move or change

look.title: The Leaf on the Pond
look.text: A student tosses a pebble into a pond and watches a leaf floating two meters away. Rings spread out from the splash. When they reach the leaf, it rises, dips, rises, dips, and then sits still again. The leaf ends up almost exactly where it started.
look.prompt: If the water itself is not traveling outward, what is? How do you know something reached the leaf?

check.q: A bump travels down a jump rope. What does the rope itself do?
choices: Each part moves up and down and returns
The rope slides toward the door
check.why: The pattern moves along the rope, but each piece of rope only moves up and down in place.

check.q: What does a wave carry from place to place?
check.why: The material stays close to where it was. The energy travels with the wave pattern.

check.q: Rings from a pebble pass a floating leaf. What happens to the leaf?
choices: It races away with the rings
It bobs up and down and stays near its spot
It is pushed back toward the splash
check.why: Water waves move the water up and down. The leaf rides those bobs but does not travel with the rings.

lessons.title: Amplitude and Wavelength
lessons.mainIdea: Amplitude is how tall a wave is, and wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next; both can be measured and drawn.
reading: Waves come in sizes. Snap the jump rope gently and a small bump travels. Snap it hard and a tall bump travels. The height of the wave above its resting line is its *amplitude*. Bigger amplitude means more energy. Ocean waves with a big amplitude are the ones that knock you over.

Now shake the rope up and down over and over. You see a chain of bumps and dips. The top of each bump is a *crest*. The distance from one crest to the next crest is the *wavelength*. Shake faster and the crests crowd together, so the wavelength gets shorter. Shake slower and it stretches out.

You can describe any wave with these two measurements. Scientists draw a wave as a wavy line. Then they label the amplitude and the wavelength. This site has a wave bench. There you can change each one and watch what happens. Try making a wave that is tall and long. Then make one that is short and small.

words.d: the height of a wave above its resting line; a measure of its energy
the highest point of a wave
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next crest

look.title: Two Drawings of Waves
look.text: Drawing A shows a wavy line with tall bumps spaced far apart. Drawing B shows a wavy line with short bumps packed close together. Both lines are the same length across the page. A student says Drawing B must carry more energy because it has more bumps.
look.prompt: Which drawing has the bigger amplitude? Which has the longer wavelength? Is the student right about energy?

check.q: What is the amplitude of a wave?
choices: Its height above the resting line
check.why: Amplitude is the height of the wave. Bigger amplitude means more energy.

check.q: You shake a rope faster. What happens to the wavelength?
check.why: Shaking faster makes crests come closer together, so the distance between them shrinks.

check.q: Which wave probably carries the most energy?
check.why: Amplitude shows energy. A tall wave has a big amplitude, so it carries more energy.

lessons.title: Waves Move Things
lessons.mainIdea: Because waves carry energy, they can make objects move, from a bobbing toy boat to a fluttering sheet of paper.
reading: Waves do work. Put a toy boat in a bathtub and slap the water at the other end. The boat rocks. Slap harder, with a bigger amplitude, and it rocks more. The energy of your slap traveled through the water and reached the boat. That is how waves make objects move.

*Sound* is a wave too. It travels through air as a pattern of pushes, a *vibration* that spreads out. Stand next to a big drum when someone strikes it. You feel the thump in your chest. Hold a sheet of paper near a loud speaker and it flutters. The air carried a wave to the paper and made it move.

Big waves can do big things. Storm waves on Lake Michigan have thrown chunks of ice and stones onto the Chicago lakefront. Earthquake waves shake the ground and can crack roads. Engineers who build harbors and bridges have to plan for the energy a wave brings.

words.d: a wave of pushes that travels through air, water or solids and that we can hear
a quick back-and-forth shaking

look.title: Speed of Sound in Different Materials
look.prompt: Rosa's taps reached Jamal through the wooden bleacher before he heard them through the air. What does this table suggest about why?

check.q: Why does a toy boat rock more when you slap the water harder?
check.why: A harder slap makes a wave with bigger amplitude, and bigger amplitude means more energy reaches the boat.

check.q: A sheet of paper flutters near a loud speaker. What moved it?
choices: A sound wave in the air
check.why: Sound is a wave of pushes in the air. The pushes reached the paper and made it move.

check.q: According to the table, in which material does sound travel fastest?
check.why: Sound travels at about 5,960 meters per second in steel, far faster than in water or air.

lessons.title: Light Bounces Into Your Eyes
lessons.mainIdea: We see an object because light from a source bounces off it and enters our eyes; with no light, we see nothing.
reading: Sit in a closet with the door shut and the light off. Wait. No matter how long you wait, you cannot see the shelf in front of you. Your eyes work fine. There is just no light. Now open the door a crack. Light slips in, hits the shelf, and *reflects* toward your eyes. Now you can see it.

To reflect means to bounce off. Light leaves a *source* like the sun, a lamp or a flashlight. It travels in straight lines until it hits something. Some of it bounces off. If the bounced light reaches your eyes, you see the object. The eye does not send anything out. It only catches light coming in.

For a long time many people believed the opposite. They thought the eyes sent out beams that felt objects. About a thousand years ago a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham argued from experiments that this could not be true. Looking at the sun hurts because light is coming in, not going out.

words.d: to bounce off a surface, as light bounces off objects
something that gives off light, like the sun or a lamp

look.title: A Book About Sight
look.text: Around the year 1020, in his Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham argued that we see because light travels from a lit object into the eye, not because the eye sends out rays. He pointed out that looking at a very bright light hurts the eye and leaves a spot in your vision afterward. That only makes sense if something is entering the eye.
look.cite: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), Book of Optics, about 1020 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Ibn al-Haytham used a painful experience as evidence. What would the old 'eye beam' idea predict instead, and why does it fail?

check.q: Why can't you see a shelf in a completely dark closet?
choices: No light is bouncing off the shelf into your eyes
The shelf is invisible in the dark
Your eyes need time to send out beams
check.why: Seeing needs light. With no source, no light reflects off the shelf, so nothing reaches your eyes.

check.q: Which of these is a light source?
check.why: A flashlight makes its own light. The moon, a mirror and a wall only reflect light from somewhere else.

check.q: What did Ibn al-Haytham argue about how we see?
choices: Eyes send out beams that touch objects
Light enters the eye from lit objects
check.why: He argued from experiments that light travels from objects into the eye, not the other way around.

lessons.title: Mirrors and Shadows
lessons.mainIdea: Light travels in straight lines, which is why mirrors show clear reflections and objects cast shadows.
reading: Shine a flashlight through a dusty room. The beam is a straight bar of light. Light does not bend around corners on its own. That is why you cannot see around a corner, and why a wall blocks a lamp. When an object blocks light, a dark patch forms behind it. That patch is a *shadow*.

A *mirror* is a very smooth, shiny surface. Light bounces off it at the same angle it came in, like a ball off a wall. Because the bounce is so neat, the light forms a clear picture. A rough surface, like paper, scatters light in every direction. You can see paper, but you cannot see yourself in it.

You can send a beam around a corner with mirrors. Point a flashlight at a mirror at the right angle and the beam turns. Add a second mirror and it turns again. A periscope uses two mirrors so a person in a submarine can see above the water. Light only goes straight, but mirrors can redirect it.

words.d: a dark patch behind an object that blocks light
a very smooth, shiny surface that reflects light in a neat, clear way

look.title: Around the Corner
look.text: A student builds a periscope from a tall cardboard tube. She fits a small mirror at the top, tilted, and another at the bottom, tilted the other way. Looking into the bottom hole, she can see over a fence that is taller than she is.
look.prompt: Trace the path of light from the top of the fence to her eye. How many times does it bounce, and why does the trick work?

check.q: Why does a wall block the light from a lamp?
choices: Light cannot bend around the wall
Light is too slow to reach the other side
The lamp is not bright enough
check.why: Light travels in straight lines. It cannot curve around the wall, so a shadow forms behind it.

check.q: Why can you see yourself in a mirror but not in a sheet of paper?
choices: Paper does not reflect any light
A mirror is smooth, so light bounces in a neat pattern
A mirror makes its own light
check.why: A smooth mirror bounces light at the same angle it came in, forming a clear picture. Paper scatters light everywhere.

check.q: A periscope uses two mirrors. What do the mirrors do to the light?
check.why: Light goes straight between bounces. Each mirror turns the beam, so two mirrors let it go up and over.

lessons.title: Light Bends in Water
lessons.mainIdea: When light passes from air into water or glass, it slows and bends; that is why a straw looks broken and a lens can focus light.
reading: Put a straw in a glass of water and look from the side. The straw looks broken at the water line. It is not. Light from the underwater part of the straw bends as it leaves the water and enters the air. Your eye follows the bent light and sees the straw in the wrong place. This bending is called *refraction*.

Light bends because it slows down when it enters water or glass. In water, light moves at about three-quarters of its speed in air. The change in speed turns the beam. Think of a shopping cart. One wheel rolls onto grass while the other stays on the sidewalk. The cart swings toward the grass. Light does the same at the edge of the water.

A *lens* is a curved piece of glass or plastic that uses refraction on purpose. A lens that bulges in the middle bends light toward a point. That is how a magnifying glass makes small things look big. It is also how the microscope and the telescope on this site work. Your own eye has a lens, too.

words.d: the bending of light when it passes from one material into another
a curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light on purpose

look.title: How Fast Light Travels
look.prompt: Light bends more when its speed changes more. Which material would bend a beam of light the most as it enters from air?

check.q: Why does a straw in water look broken?
choices: Light bends as it leaves the water
check.why: Refraction bends the light from the underwater part, so your eye sees that part in the wrong place.

check.q: What happens to light when it enters water from air?
check.why: Light travels slower in water than in air. The change in speed makes the beam turn.

check.q: What does a magnifying glass do to light?
choices: Blocks it to make a shadow
check.why: A lens that bulges in the middle refracts light toward a point, which makes small things look big.

lessons.title: Dots, Dashes and Blinks
lessons.mainIdea: A code turns letters into a pattern of short and long signals, so a flashlight or a wire can carry words.
reading: A *code* is an agreement about what patterns mean. In the 1830s and 1840s, Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail built a code out of short and long electric pulses. A short pulse is a dot. A long one is a dash. The letter S is three dots. The letter O is three dashes. Together, they spell the emergency call SOS.

In 1844, Morse sent the first public message over a wire from Washington to Baltimore. The pulses arrived almost at once. Before that, a letter took days. Within a few years, telegraph wires reached Chicago, and news could cross Illinois in minutes. A *signal* is any pattern sent to carry a message.

Morse code works with anything that can be on or off. A flashlight can blink it. A whistle can chirp it. Ships still use signal lamps to flash it between decks. The wave that carries it does not matter, as long as the sender and the receiver agree on the code.

words.d: an agreement about what each pattern of signals means
a pattern sent from one place to another to carry a message

look.title: The First Public Telegraph Message
look.cite: Samuel F. B. Morse, telegraph message sent from Washington to Baltimore, May 24, 1844
look.prompt: These four words crossed about 40 miles of wire in an instant as electric pulses. What had to be true at both ends of the wire for the message to be read?

check.q: In Morse code, what is the letter S?
check.why: S is three short signals, or dots. O is three long signals, or dashes.

check.q: Why can a flashlight send Morse code?
choices: Because light is faster than electricity
Because it can be turned on and off in a pattern
Because light is a kind of wire
check.why: Morse code needs only short and long signals. A flashlight can blink short and long.

check.q: What must be true for a coded message to work?
choices: The signal must be very loud
Sender and receiver must agree on the code
The wire must be made of copper
check.why: A code is an agreement. If the receiver does not know the code, the pattern is just noise.

lessons.title: Drum Talk
lessons.mainIdea: Beats on a drum can carry a message across a distance because people agree on what each pattern means.
reading: Long before wires, people sent messages with sound. In parts of West Africa, drummers used special drums to send news from village to village. A trained listener far away could hear the *rhythm* and understand it. Rhythm is a *pattern* of beats and pauses in time. The sound wave carried the pattern through the air.

A drum message has parts you can change. You can hit hard or soft, which changes the amplitude of the sound wave. You can hit fast or slow. You can leave long gaps or short ones. Each choice is a piece of the pattern. Put the pieces together and you have a signal.

Try it with a partner and the drum bench on this site, or a desk and your hands. Agree on three patterns: one for yes, one for no, one for help. Then turn your backs and send messages. If the patterns are too alike, mistakes happen. Good codes use patterns that are easy to tell apart.

words.d: a pattern of beats and pauses in time
something that repeats or follows a rule you can recognize

look.title: Two Codes
look.text: Team A decides that 'yes' is two taps and 'no' is three taps. Team B decides that 'yes' is two quick taps and 'no' is one slow, heavy thump. Across a noisy room, Team A keeps getting messages wrong. Team B almost never does.
look.prompt: Why does Team B's code work better in a noisy room? What makes two patterns easy to tell apart?

check.q: What carries a drum message from one village to another?
choices: A sound wave through the air
check.why: The drum makes a sound wave. The wave travels through the air and carries the rhythm.

check.q: Hitting the drum harder changes which part of the sound wave?
check.why: A harder hit makes a louder sound, which means a sound wave with bigger amplitude.

check.q: Why should code patterns be very different from each other?
choices: So they take longer to send
So the receiver does not mix them up
check.why: Patterns that are too alike are easy to confuse, especially when there is noise.

lessons.title: Ones and Zeros
lessons.mainIdea: Computers send pictures, sounds and words as long strings of just two signals, on and off, called binary.
reading: A phone or a computer sends everything as *binary*. Binary uses only two signals, written as 1 and 0. A 1 can be a flash of light, a pulse of electricity or a burst of radio. A 0 is a gap. Each 1 or 0 is called a *bit*. Bits are the smallest pieces of a *digital* message.

How can two signals say anything? By making patterns. With one bit you can make two patterns: 1 or 0. With two bits you get four: 00, 01, 10, 11. Every extra bit doubles the count. Eight bits make 256 patterns, enough for every letter, number and mark on a keyboard. The letter A, for example, is 01000001.

Every photo you have ever sent was a long string of bits. Some traveled as flashes of light down a glass thread thinner than a hair. Some traveled as radio waves from a Wi-Fi router. Some ran as electric pulses along copper wires. Different waves, same code: on and off, over and over, very fast.

words.d: a code that uses only two signals, written as 1 and 0
a single 1 or 0, the smallest piece of a digital message
made of separate on-or-off signals rather than a smooth, changing one

look.title: How Many Patterns Bits Can Make
look.cite: counting rule: each added bit doubles the number of patterns
look.prompt: Find the rule in the numbers. How many patterns could 5 bits make? Why are 8 bits enough for every key on a keyboard?

check.q: How many different signals does binary use?
check.why: Binary uses only two signals, 1 and 0, which can be on and off.

check.q: With 3 bits, how many patterns can you make?
check.why: Each added bit doubles the count: 2, then 4, then 8.

check.q: Which wave can carry binary?
choices: Any of these, as long as it can be on or off
check.why: Binary needs only an on-and-off signal. Light, radio and electric pulses can all do that.

lessons.title: Clean Signals Over Long Distances
lessons.mainIdea: Digital signals of on and off can be copied and sent again without mistakes, which is why they carry messages so far.
reading: Every wave gets weaker as it travels. Shout across a field and your voice fades. Along the way, other sounds mix in. Scientists call this unwanted mix *noise*. A soft, smooth signal like a voice is hard to fix once noise gets in. You cannot tell which wobbles were the message.

A digital signal is different. The *receiver* only has to decide one thing: was that on or off? Even a weak, fuzzy flash is clearly not a gap. So a receiver can read the bits, make a fresh, strong copy, and send it on. Do this every few miles and the message crosses an ocean as clean as it started.

That is why a text from Chicago reaches a friend in another country without a single wrong letter. It is also why Jamal's flashlight worked across a noisy gym. Rosa never had to hear his voice. She only had to see light or no light. Simple patterns are hard to break.

words.d: unwanted signals that mix into a message and make it harder to read
the person or machine that takes in a signal and reads it

look.title: The Fading Whisper
look.text: Twenty students stand in a line. The first whispers a sentence to the next, and so on. By the end, the sentence is nonsense. Then they try again with a rule: only tap once for yes or twice for no. This time the last student gets every answer right, even with a loud fan running.
look.prompt: Why did the tapping game survive the line and the fan when the whisper did not? How is this like a digital signal?

check.q: What is noise, in this lesson?
choices: Unwanted signals mixed into a message
check.why: Noise is anything that gets mixed into a signal and makes the real message harder to read.

check.q: Why can a weak digital signal still be read correctly?
choices: The receiver only has to tell on from off
check.why: Even a fuzzy flash is clearly on, not off. That simple choice makes bits easy to read and copy.

check.q: Why did the flashlight message work in a noisy gym?
choices: The signal was a simple on-or-off pattern
check.why: Rosa only needed to see light or no light. Noise in the gym could not change that pattern.

review.q: A wave passes a floating duck. The duck:
choices: Bobs up and down and stays near its spot
review.why: Water waves move water up and down. The wave pattern travels on, but the duck stays close to where it was.

choices: The distance from one crest to the next
review.why: Wavelength is the distance between neighboring crests. Amplitude is the height.

review.q: You feel a drum thump in your chest. What reached you?
review.why: Sound is a wave of pushes through the air. Its energy can move your chest and a sheet of paper.

review.q: You see a red apple because:
choices: Your eyes send beams to the apple
The apple makes its own light
Red is a kind of sound
Light bounces off the apple into your eyes
review.why: Light from a source reflects off the apple. Some of that light enters your eyes.

review.q: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent because:
choices: Light bends when it moves from water to air
The water pushes on the pencil
Your eyes get confused by wet things
review.why: Refraction bends the light leaving the water, so your eye sees the underwater part in the wrong place.

choices: Three dashes, three dots, three dashes
Three dots, three dashes, three dots
review.why: S is three dots and O is three dashes, so SOS is dot-dot-dot, dash-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot.

review.q: Which best describes a digital signal?
choices: A message that must be shouted
A pattern made of on-and-off signals
review.why: Digital signals use separate on-or-off pieces, called bits, instead of a smooth changing wave.

review.q: Why can digital messages travel across an ocean without errors?
choices: The message is sent only once
Receivers copy the bits fresh and send them on
review.why: A receiver only decides on or off, then makes a strong new copy. Noise cannot pile up.
